questions.title: SQL Query Execution Order
questions.question: In what order does SQL actually execute the clauses in a SELECT statement?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Logical order: FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT
- WHERE filters before grouping; HAVING filters after grouping
- SELECT aliases not available in WHERE because SELECT runs after WHERE
- Aggregate functions not allowed in WHERE (run HAVING instead)
- ORDER BY is the last step — most expensive for large result sets
- Red flag: confusing WHERE and HAVING, or using aggregates in WHERE

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
SQL executes clauses in a specific logical order that's different from how you write the query. The engine starts with FROM and JOIN to assemble the full dataset, then WHERE to filter individual rows before any grouping happens, then GROUP BY to aggregate, then HAVING to filter those aggregated results. Only after all that does SELECT run to pick which columns you want, followed by ORDER BY and finally LIMIT.

This matters practically because it explains common errors. You cannot use a SELECT alias in your WHERE clause because WHERE runs before SELECT evaluates that alias. You cannot put aggregate functions like COUNT or AVG directly in a WHERE clause because grouping hasn't happened yet — use HAVING for that.

Understanding this order makes you a much faster debugger. When you see an error about aggregate functions in WHERE, you immediately know the fix is to move the condition to HAVING. When an alias doesn't resolve, you know to repeat the expression or use a subquery.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Logical Execution Order

```sql
SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal   -- 6: evaluate columns
FROM employees                               -- 1: start here
JOIN departments USING (dept_id)             -- 2: apply joins
WHERE hire_date > '2020-01-01'              -- 3: filter rows (before grouping)
GROUP BY department                         -- 4: aggregate into groups
HAVING AVG(salary) > 80000                  -- 5: filter groups
ORDER BY avg_sal DESC                       -- 7: sort
LIMIT 10;                                   -- 8: cut
```

## Common Mistakes This Prevents

```sql
-- WRONG: aggregate in WHERE
SELECT department, COUNT(*) FROM employees
WHERE COUNT(*) > 5 GROUP BY department; -- Error!

-- RIGHT: use HAVING
SELECT department, COUNT(*) FROM employees
GROUP BY department HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

-- WRONG: alias in WHERE
SELECT salary * 1.1 AS new_salary FROM employees
WHERE new_salary > 100000; -- Error!

-- RIGHT: repeat the expression
SELECT salary * 1.1 AS new_salary FROM employees
WHERE salary * 1.1 > 100000;
```

## Performance Insight
Filter early with WHERE — fewer rows to group means less work in GROUP BY. Use HAVING only for conditions that genuinely require the aggregate result.

speakable_v2.hook: SQL executes clauses in a specific logical order that's different from how you write the query.
speakable_v2.cap: When an alias doesn't resolve, you know to repeat the expression or use a subquery.

questions.title: SQL JOIN Types Explained
questions.question: What are the different types of SQL JOINs and when do you use each one?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- INNER JOIN: only rows matching in both tables
- LEFT JOIN: all rows from left, NULLs for unmatched right side
- RIGHT JOIN: opposite (usually rewritten as LEFT for clarity)
- FULL OUTER JOIN: all rows from both, NULLs where no match
- CROSS JOIN: cartesian product — every row combined with every other row
- Anti-join pattern: LEFT JOIN + WHERE right.id IS NULL to find rows without a match
- Self join: joining a table to itself for hierarchy or comparison queries

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
INNER JOIN returns only rows where the join condition matches in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table regardless of whether there is a match on the right — unmatched rows get NULL in the right table's columns. Right and full outer joins follow the same logic in their respective directions.

The most useful pattern to know beyond the basics is the anti-join: a LEFT JOIN where you filter for WHERE right_table.id IS NULL. This finds rows in the left table that have no corresponding row in the right table — for example, customers who have never placed an order.

Self-joins are also worth mentioning. You join a table to itself using two aliases, which is how you compare rows within the same table — like finding all employees who earn more than their own manager.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## JOIN Types at a Glance

```
A = {1,2,3}  B = {2,3,4}

INNER JOIN → {2,3}         only matching
LEFT JOIN  → {1,2,3}       all A, NULL for A rows without B match
RIGHT JOIN → {2,3,4}       all B, NULL for B rows without A match
FULL JOIN  → {1,2,3,4}     everything, NULLs where no match
```

## Practical Patterns

```sql
-- Anti-join: customers with NO orders
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

-- Self-join: employees earning more than manager
SELECT e.name, e.salary, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

-- Multi-table join
SELECT o.id, c.name AS customer, p.title AS product
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN products  p ON o.product_id  = p.id
WHERE o.status = 'pending';
```

## CROSS JOIN (use carefully)

```sql
-- Every size paired with every colour — 3x4 = 12 rows
SELECT s.name AS size, c.name AS colour
FROM sizes s CROSS JOIN colours c;
-- Common in generating all combinations for reports or seeding data
```

speakable_v2.hook: INNER JOIN returns only rows where the join condition matches in both tables.
speakable_v2.cap: You join a table to itself using two aliases, which is how you compare rows within the same table — like finding all employees who earn more than their own manager.

questions.title: SQL Aggregate Functions
questions.question: What are SQL aggregate functions and how do you use GROUP BY and HAVING with them?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Core aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX — collapse multiple rows into one
- COUNT(*) counts all rows including NULLs; COUNT(column) skips NULLs
- GROUP BY: defines which column(s) to aggregate around
- All non-aggregate columns in SELECT must appear in GROUP BY
- HAVING: filters after aggregation (like WHERE for groups)
- DISTINCT inside aggregate: COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts unique values
- GROUP BY ROLLUP / CUBE for subtotals

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Aggregate functions collapse a group of rows into a single value. The five core ones are COUNT for row counting, SUM for totals, AVG for averages, and MIN/MAX for extremes. GROUP BY is what defines the groupings — without it, aggregates run over the entire result set as one big group.

A common mistake is putting non-aggregated columns in the SELECT that aren't in the GROUP BY. If you select department and salary together without grouping, which salary should the database show for a department with fifty employees? SQL forces you to either aggregate salary or include it in GROUP BY.

HAVING is the WHERE clause for groups. WHERE runs before aggregation and can't reference aggregate results. HAVING runs after aggregation and filters based on aggregate values — so HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 keeps only departments with more than five employees.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Core Aggregates

```sql
SELECT
    department,
    COUNT(*)                    AS total_employees,
    COUNT(DISTINCT manager_id)  AS num_managers,
    SUM(salary)                 AS payroll,
    AVG(salary)                 AS avg_salary,
    MIN(salary)                 AS lowest,
    MAX(salary)                 AS highest
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5          -- only depts with 5+ employees
ORDER BY payroll DESC;
```

## COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)

```sql
-- COUNT(*): counts ALL rows, including NULLs
-- COUNT(col): counts rows where col IS NOT NULL
SELECT COUNT(*)           AS total_rows,  -- 100
       COUNT(phone_number) AS with_phone,  -- 73 (if 27 have NULL phone)
       COUNT(DISTINCT city) AS unique_cities
FROM customers;
```

## Grouping Sets / Rollup

```sql
-- ROLLUP adds subtotal rows automatically
SELECT department, job_title, SUM(salary)
FROM employees
GROUP BY ROLLUP (department, job_title);
-- Produces: per (dept, job), per dept subtotal, and grand total
```

## FILTER Clause (PostgreSQL)

```sql
-- Conditional aggregation
SELECT department,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE salary > 80000) AS high_earners,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE salary <= 80000) AS regular
FROM employees
GROUP BY department;
```

speakable_v2.hook: Aggregate functions collapse a group of rows into a single value.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: HAVING runs after aggregation and filters based on aggregate values — so HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 keeps only departments with more than five employees.

questions.title: SQL Window Functions
questions.question: What are SQL window functions and how do they differ from aggregate functions?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Window functions compute over a set of related rows but keep each row (no collapsing)
- OVER() clause is required — defines the window: PARTITION BY + ORDER BY
- ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), DENSE_RANK() for row numbering within groups
- LAG(), LEAD() for accessing previous/next row values
- SUM/AVG OVER for running totals and moving averages
- ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING for cumulative calculations
- Classic pattern: top-N rows per group using ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The fundamental difference from aggregate functions is what happens to your rows. Aggregate functions collapse a group of rows into one. Window functions compute across a group of related rows but return a value for every individual row — your dataset stays intact.

The OVER clause is what makes a function a window function. PARTITION BY divides your data into groups — like GROUP BY but without collapsing. ORDER BY inside OVER defines the sequence for running calculations. Without ORDER BY, functions like ROW_NUMBER or RANK don't have a defined order to work with.

The classic interview question about window functions is getting the top three earners per department. Without window functions you need a complex self-join or subquery. With window functions you add a computed column using ROW_NUMBER partitioned by department and ordered by salary descending, then wrap it and filter where that row number is three or less. Clean and readable.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Aggregate vs Window

```sql
-- Aggregate: one row per department
SELECT department, AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department;

-- Window: every employee row plus their dept average
SELECT name, department, salary,
       AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department)          AS dept_avg,
       salary - AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS diff_from_avg
FROM employees;
```

## Ranking Functions

```sql
SELECT name, salary,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS row_num,    -- unique, no ties
  RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk,        -- ties share rank, gaps after
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dense_rnk   -- ties share rank, no gaps
FROM employees;
-- salary: 100, 90, 90, 80
-- ROW_NUMBER:  1,  2,  3,  4
-- RANK:        1,  2,  2,  4
-- DENSE_RANK:  1,  2,  2,  3
```

## Top-N Per Group

```sql
SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn
    FROM employees
) t WHERE rn <= 3;  -- top 3 earners in each department
```

## LAG / LEAD and Running Totals

```sql
-- Day-over-day revenue change
SELECT date, revenue,
  LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY date)         AS prev_day,
  revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY date) AS change
FROM daily_sales;

-- Running total
SELECT date, revenue,
  SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS cumulative
FROM daily_sales;
```

speakable_v2.hook: The fundamental difference from aggregate functions is what happens to your rows.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

questions.title: SQL Indexes and Query Performance
questions.question: How do database indexes work and when should you add or avoid them?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- B-tree index: sorted structure enabling O(log n) lookup vs O(n) table scan
- Trade-off: faster reads, slower writes — every write must update all indexes
- When to index: high-cardinality columns, foreign keys, WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY columns
- When not to index: booleans, low-cardinality, small tables, write-heavy tables
- Composite index column order matters: leftmost prefix rule
- Covering index: includes all columns a query needs, avoiding a table lookup
- Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to confirm index usage

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
An index is a separate sorted data structure that allows the database to find rows without scanning every one. Think of it as the index at the back of a textbook — instead of reading every page, you find the topic alphabetically and jump directly to the right pages. For a million-row table this is the difference between one lookup and a million comparisons.

The cost is write performance. Every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE must update all affected indexes to stay consistent. A table with ten indexes is significantly slower to write to than one with no indexes, so you index selectively based on actual query patterns rather than preemptively.

Composite indexes have a leftmost prefix rule that trips people up. An index on department, salary, hire_date can serve queries filtering on department, or on department and salary, but not on salary alone. Think of it like a phone book — sorted by last name then first name. You can look up Smith, or Smith John, but you cannot efficiently search for all Johns without knowing their last name.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Index Types

| Type | Best For |
|------|----------|
| B-tree (default) | Equality, range, sorting |
| Hash | Equality only |
| GIN (PostgreSQL) | JSONB, arrays, full-text |
| Partial | Subset of rows |

## Composite Index — Column Order Matters

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_emp ON employees (department, salary);

-- USES index (starts with leftmost column)
WHERE department = 'Eng';
WHERE department = 'Eng' AND salary > 90000;

-- CANNOT use this index (no leftmost column)
WHERE salary > 90000;  -- full scan
```

## Covering Index — No Table Lookup

```sql
-- Query only needs these three columns
SELECT department, salary, hire_date FROM employees
WHERE department = 'Engineering';

-- A covering index satisfies this entirely without touching the table
CREATE INDEX idx_covering ON employees (department, salary, hire_date);
```

## Partial Index — Index Only What You Query

```sql
-- 95% of orders are 'completed' — only index the active minority
CREATE INDEX idx_active_orders ON orders (created_at)
WHERE status IN ('pending', 'processing');

-- Tiny index, very fast for: WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY created_at
```

## Check Index Usage

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE department = 'Engineering';
-- Look for: Index Scan vs Seq Scan
-- High filter rows removed = index could help more
```

speakable_v2.hook: An index is a separate sorted data structure that allows the database to find rows without scanning every one.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: You can look up Smith, or Smith John, but you cannot efficiently search for all Johns without knowing their last name.

questions.title: ACID Properties and Transaction Isolation
questions.question: What are ACID properties in databases and how do isolation levels work?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- A=Atomicity (all or nothing), C=Consistency (valid state always), I=Isolation (no interference), D=Durability (survives crash)
- Isolation levels: READ UNCOMMITTED → READ COMMITTED → REPEATABLE READ → SERIALIZABLE
- Each level prevents more anomalies: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read
- PostgreSQL default: READ COMMITTED; MySQL InnoDB default: REPEATABLE READ
- Spring @Transactional: defaults to database default isolation
- Trade-off: stronger isolation = fewer anomalies but more locking and lower concurrency

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
ACID is the set of guarantees that make databases reliable. Atomicity means all or nothing — transferring money debits one account and credits another, and if anything fails, neither change sticks. Consistency means every transaction leaves the database in a state that satisfies all defined rules and constraints. Isolation means concurrent transactions don't see each other's in-progress work. Durability means once committed, data survives even an immediate server crash.

Isolation is the most nuanced because different levels trade correctness for concurrency. READ COMMITTED, PostgreSQL's default, prevents dirty reads but allows non-repeatable reads — the same row might return different values if you read it twice within one transaction because another transaction updated it between your reads. REPEATABLE READ prevents that but allows phantom reads where new rows appear. SERIALIZABLE eliminates all anomalies but uses the most locking.

In practice, READ COMMITTED covers most web applications. You step up to SERIALIZABLE or REPEATABLE READ only when business logic requires a consistent view of multiple rows across multiple queries — like generating a financial report where all numbers must reflect the same point in time.

questions.title: Database Normalization
questions.question: What is database normalization and when should you intentionally denormalize?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Normalization: organizing data to reduce redundancy and improve consistency
- 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups
- 2NF: no partial dependencies on composite key
- 3NF: no transitive dependencies (non-key depends on non-key)
- Benefits: no update anomalies, less storage, consistent data
- When to denormalize: read-heavy analytics, reporting, when joins become bottlenecks
- Star/snowflake schema in data warehouses is intentionally denormalized for read speed

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Normalization is the process of organizing your database to eliminate redundant data and ensure each piece of information is stored in exactly one place. The practical benefit is consistency — if a customer changes their address, you update one row in the customers table rather than updating that address everywhere it appears in dozens of order rows.

The normal forms — first, second, third — are progressively stricter rules about where data lives. Third Normal Form is usually where most transactional databases should land: every non-key column depends only on the primary key, not on other non-key columns. A zip code determining a city and state is a transitive dependency — the city should live in a zip codes table.

Denormalization is a deliberate performance trade-off. In read-heavy analytics or reporting systems, joining five tables to answer every query becomes a bottleneck. You intentionally store redundant data — maybe copying the customer name into each order row — to avoid joins at read time. The trade-off is that updates become more complex and you need to keep the redundant copies in sync.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Normal Forms

**1NF**: Each column holds atomic values, no repeating groups
```sql
-- WRONG: comma-separated phones in one column
CREATE TABLE customers (id INT, phones VARCHAR(200)); -- '555-1234,555-5678'

-- RIGHT: separate table for phones
CREATE TABLE customer_phones (customer_id INT, phone VARCHAR(20));
```

**2NF**: No partial dependency (applies to composite PKs)
```sql
-- WRONG: product_name depends only on product_id, not on (order_id, product_id)
CREATE TABLE order_items (order_id INT, product_id INT, product_name TEXT, quantity INT);

-- RIGHT: product_name belongs in products table
CREATE TABLE order_items (order_id INT, product_id INT, quantity INT);
CREATE TABLE products (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, price NUMERIC);
```

**3NF**: No transitive dependency
```sql
-- WRONG: city depends on zip, not directly on customer_id
CREATE TABLE customers (id INT, zip VARCHAR(10), city TEXT, state TEXT);

-- RIGHT: extract zip code data to its own table
CREATE TABLE customers (id INT, zip VARCHAR(10));
CREATE TABLE zip_codes (zip VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY, city TEXT, state TEXT);
```

## When to Denormalize

| Scenario | Approach |
|----------|-----------|
| OLTP (transactions) | Normalize to 3NF |
| OLAP (analytics) | Star schema (denormalized) |
| Read-heavy API | Materialized views |
| Report generation | Dedicated read replica with precomputed tables |

speakable_v2.hook: Normalization is the process of organizing your database to eliminate redundant data and ensure each piece of information is stored in exactly one place.
speakable_v2.cap: The trade-off is that updates become more complex and you need to keep the redundant copies in sync.

questions.title: Stored Procedures, Views, and Triggers
questions.question: What are SQL stored procedures, views, and triggers — when should you use them in a Java application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- View: named saved query — simplifies complex queries, adds access control layer
- Materialized view: stored result of a query — fast reads, must refresh for fresh data
- Stored procedure: logic stored in the DB — reduces round trips but harder to version/test
- Trigger: auto-runs SQL on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE events
- Modern Java teams prefer application-layer logic over stored procedures (testability, version control)
- Materialized views excellent for expensive read queries (dashboard aggregates)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A view is a saved SELECT query that you can query like a table. It doesn't store data — every time you select from a view, it re-runs the underlying query. Views are useful for simplifying complex joins into a meaningful name, and for restricting what columns certain roles can see without duplicating data.

Materialized views do store the result. They're like a cached query result on disk. They can be indexed and queried very fast, but they show data as of the last refresh. This makes them excellent for expensive dashboard aggregations that don't need to be real-time — you refresh them on a schedule.

Stored procedures are SQL logic stored in the database itself. They were popular when database roundtrips were expensive and application servers were slow. Modern Java teams generally avoid complex business logic in stored procedures because they're harder to unit test, harder to version control, and create tight coupling to the database vendor. Use them when reducing roundtrips matters, like batch processing large datasets where pushing the loop into the database avoids shipping thousands of rows to the application.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: A view is a saved SELECT query that you can query like a table.
speakable_v2.cap: Use them when reducing roundtrips matters, like batch processing large datasets where pushing the loop into the database avoids shipping thousands of rows to the application.
